t: The three classic criteria against which any investment made by an insurer is judged are:
o: Safety, liquidity and return
Commission, brand and size
Tax, tenure and listing
Coupon, rating and custodian
e: Insurers evaluate investments on safety (security of capital), liquidity (ability to realise cash when needed) and yield (return), in that order of priority.

t: An insurer with a positive duration gap (asset duration greater than liability duration) would benefit from:
o: A rise in interest rates
No change in interest rates
A fall in interest rates
A steepening of the yield curve only
e: With assets more rate-sensitive than liabilities, falling rates raise assets more than liabilities, widening the surplus; rising rates would hurt.

t: Which of the following is an advantage of investing in equity shares as compared with fixed-coupon bonds?
o: A contractually fixed income every year
Potential for capital appreciation and a hedge against inflation over the long run
Priority over creditors in the event of winding up
Freedom from price volatility
e: Equity carries residual ownership rights and participates in growth, offering inflation protection over time; bonds give fixed income and rank ahead of equity on liquidation.

t: Public Provident Fund, National Savings Certificates and Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme are examples of:
o: Money market instruments issued by banks
Exchange-traded derivatives
Government-sponsored small savings instruments with sovereign backing
Alternative investment funds regulated by SEBI
e: These small savings schemes are offered by the Government of India through post offices and banks, with administered interest rates and sovereign backing.

t: The term 'free-float market capitalisation' refers to:
o: Market capitalisation computed only on shares readily available for trading, excluding promoter and locked-in holdings
Total shares issued multiplied by the face value
Market capitalisation including all shares held by promoters
The value of shares traded on a single day
e: Major Indian indices such as Nifty 50 and Sensex use free-float capitalisation so that stocks are weighted by their investable portion.

t: Settlement of equity trades on Indian stock exchanges currently takes place on a:
o: T+1 rolling settlement basis
T+5 rolling settlement basis
Weekly account period basis
T+3 rolling settlement basis
e: SEBI moved the Indian equity cash market fully to T+1 settlement in January 2023 (with an optional T+0 segment introduced later).

t: A company has net profit of ₹240 crore and 60 crore equity shares outstanding. Its share trades at ₹120. The price-earnings (P/E) ratio is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). EPS = 240/60 = ₹4; P/E = Price/EPS = 120/4 = 30 times.

t: Return on Equity (ROE) is computed as:
o: Net profit divided by total assets
Operating profit divided by sales
Dividend divided by market price
Net profit after tax divided by shareholders' equity
e: ROE = PAT / Shareholders' funds, measuring the return generated on owners' capital; PAT/total assets is ROA.

t: A company has sales of ₹2,000 crore, net profit margin of 8% and total assets of ₹1,600 crore financed 50% by equity. Using the DuPont framework, its return on equity is:
When a short-term moving average (e.g. 50-day) crosses above a long-term moving average (e.g. 200-day), technical analysts generally regard this as:
o: A bearish signal (often called a death cross)
A bullish signal (often called a golden cross)
A signal that the company will cut its dividend
Evidence that the market is strong-form efficient
e: A golden cross suggests upward momentum; the reverse crossover (short-term falling below long-term) is a bearish death cross.

t: The Relative Strength Index (RSI) is an oscillator that ranges between 0 and 100; a reading above 70 is conventionally read as:
o: Overbought, suggesting a possible price correction
Oversold, suggesting a possible rebound
A neutral market with no trend
A buy signal in all circumstances
e: RSI above 70 is taken as overbought and below 30 as oversold; these are indicative thresholds rather than guarantees.

t: Strategic asset allocation differs from tactical asset allocation in that strategic allocation:
o: Changes weights daily in response to price movements
Is used only by individual investors
Applies only to the equity portion of the portfolio
Sets long-term policy weights for asset classes based on objectives and risk tolerance, whereas tactical allocation makes short-term deviations to exploit market views
e: Strategic allocation is the long-run policy mix; tactical allocation temporarily over- or under-weights classes relative to that policy.

t: A life insurer with long-dated participating liabilities and a strong solvency position is, other things equal, best placed to:
o: Hold its entire portfolio in overnight money market instruments
Avoid government securities entirely
Invest only in instruments maturing within one year
Hold a higher allocation to long-term bonds and some equity, given its long horizon and capacity to absorb volatility
e: Long liabilities and surplus capital allow a longer investment horizon and some risk-taking; an all-cash or all-short portfolio would create a serious duration mismatch.

t: The investment pattern applicable to a general insurer under the IRDAI Investment Regulations caps investments in 'other investments' at:
o: 25% of investment assets
15% of investment assets
35% of investment assets
30% of investment assets
e: General insurers may hold approved investments and other investments together up to 70%, with 'other investments' not exceeding 15% of investment assets.

t: Which of the following must an insurer appoint under IRDAI investment norms for the safe keeping and settlement of its securities?
o: A merchant banker
A stock broker as sole custodian
The Appointed Actuary
A SEBI-registered custodian independent of the insurer's promoter group
e: Insurers must hold securities in dematerialised form with an independent custodian; the custodian should not be a promoter-group entity.

t: A life insurer with a life fund of ₹40,000 crore holds ₹9,000 crore in Central Government securities, ₹12,000 crore in State Government and other approved securities, ₹6,500 crore in housing and infrastructure, and the balance in approved and other investments. Which pattern requirement is breached?
o: The 50% minimum in government and other approved securities
The 25% minimum in Central Government securities, since ₹9,000 crore is only 22.5%
The 15% minimum in housing and infrastructure
No requirement is breached

t: An insurer's Available Solvency Margin is ₹1,800 crore and its Required Solvency Margin is ₹1,000 crore. The solvency ratio is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Solvency ratio = ASM / RSM = 1,800 / 1,000 = 1.80 or 180%, which is above the 150% control level.

t: Under IRDAI norms, the Investment Committee of an insurer is required to meet at least:
o: Once a month
Once a year
Once every quarter
Once every half year
e: The Investment Committee must meet at least once a quarter to review investment policy implementation, risk management and compliance.

t: Which section of the Insurance Act, 1938 requires every insurer to maintain an excess of the value of assets over liabilities (the solvency margin)?
o: Section 64VA
Section 27A
Section 40B
Section 2(9)
e: Section 64VA deals with sufficiency of assets and the solvency margin; Section 27A deals with investment of life insurer's funds.

t: IRDAI's Asset-Liability Management and stress testing requirements require life insurers to:
o: Hold only cash to pass the stress test
Discontinue the sale of participating policies
Obtain a bank guarantee equal to their liabilities
Project assets and liabilities under adverse scenarios and report the impact on solvency periodically
e: Stress testing under ALM examines solvency under interest-rate, equity, lapse and mortality shocks; results are reported to IRDAI with the actuarial valuation.

topic: Fixed Income and Money Market Instruments
t: A State Development Loan (SDL) is a:
o: Loan given by banks to state-owned enterprises
Short-term bill issued by the Central Government
Bond issued by a municipal corporation
Dated security issued by a State Government through RBI auctions
e: SDLs are State Government market borrowings; they are 'approved securities' and carry a small yield spread over Central Government securities.

topic: Fixed Income and Money Market Instruments
t: Which of the following is a feature of a floating rate bond?
o: Its coupon is reset periodically with reference to a benchmark rate, so its price is less sensitive to interest rate changes
It pays no coupon and is issued at a deep discount
Its coupon is fixed for life but principal varies with inflation
It can never be redeemed before maturity
e: Floaters reset coupons (e.g. to T-bill yields plus a spread), keeping their price close to par; zero-coupon bonds are issued at a discount and inflation-indexed bonds adjust principal.

topic: Fixed Income and Money Market Instruments
t: The call money market in India deals in borrowing and lending of funds for:
o: 7 to 14 days
Overnight (one day)
Three months to one year
One to five years
e: Call money is overnight inter-bank lending; notice money covers 2 to 14 days and term money exceeds 14 days.

topic: Fixed Income and Money Market Instruments
t: A bond is 'callable' when:
o: The holder can demand early redemption from the issuer
The issuer has the right to redeem it before maturity at a pre-specified price
It can be converted into equity shares at the holder's option
It is listed on a stock exchange
e: A call option benefits the issuer (typically exercised when rates fall); a put option gives the holder the right to demand early redemption.

t: The standard deviation of returns is a measure of:
o: The average return earned over the period
The correlation between two securities
The sensitivity of return to the market
The dispersion of actual returns around the expected return
e: Standard deviation (square root of variance) quantifies total risk as the spread of outcomes around the mean.

t: Annual returns on a security over three years were 10%, −4% and 15%. The arithmetic mean return is:
e: Arithmetic mean = (10 − 4 + 15)/3 = 21/3 = 7%. The geometric mean would be slightly lower, about 6.6%.

t: An investor who demands a higher expected return for taking on additional risk is described as:
o: Risk averse
Risk neutral
Risk seeking
Risk indifferent
e: Risk-averse investors require compensation (a risk premium) for bearing risk; risk-neutral investors care only about expected return.

t: The efficient frontier in Markowitz portfolio theory consists of portfolios that:
o: Contain only government securities
Offer the highest expected return for each level of risk (or lowest risk for each level of return)
Have zero correlation with the market
Offer the highest return irrespective of risk
e: Efficient portfolios dominate all others in the risk-return space; a rational investor chooses from this frontier according to risk tolerance.

t: A fund earned 14% over the year with a standard deviation of 10%; the risk-free rate was 6%. Its Sharpe ratio is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Sharpe ratio = (Rp − Rf)/σp = (14 − 6)/10 = 0.80. It measures excess return per unit of total risk.

t: The Capital Market Line (CML) differs from the Security Market Line (SML) in that the CML:
o: Plots expected return against beta for all securities
Is downward sloping
Plots expected return against total risk (standard deviation) for efficient portfolios only
Applies only to risk-free securities
e: The CML relates return to standard deviation for combinations of the risk-free asset and the market portfolio; the SML relates return to beta for any asset.

t: The market risk premium under CAPM is:
o: Risk-free rate minus inflation
Expected market return minus the risk-free rate
Beta multiplied by the risk-free rate
The dividend yield of the market index
e: Market risk premium = E(Rm) − Rf, the extra return investors require for holding the market portfolio rather than the risk-free asset.

t: Portfolio P returned 15% with beta 1.5 and Portfolio Q returned 12% with beta 0.8; the risk-free rate is 6%. Based on the Treynor ratio, which portfolio performed better?
o: P, with a Treynor ratio of 6.0 versus 7.5 for Q
Both performed equally
Q, with a Treynor ratio of 7.5 versus 6.0 for P
P, because its absolute return is higher
e: Treynor = (Rp − Rf)/β: P = (15 − 6)/1.5 = 6.0; Q = (12 − 6)/0.8 = 7.5. Q delivered more excess return per unit of systematic risk.

t: The time-weighted rate of return is preferred over the money-weighted (IRR) return for evaluating a fund manager because it:
o: Gives more weight to periods with larger investments
Is easier to compute for a single lump-sum investment
Eliminates the effect of the timing and size of cash inflows and outflows, which the manager does not control
Always produces a higher return figure
e: TWRR chains sub-period returns so that investor-driven cash flows do not distort the measure of the manager's skill.

t: The earnings yield of a share is:
o: Dividend divided by market price
Market price divided by EPS
EPS divided by market price, i.e. the reciprocal of the P/E ratio
Net profit divided by book value
e: Earnings yield = EPS/Price = 1/(P/E); it is often compared with bond yields to judge relative valuation.

t: A company's equity shares trade at ₹480 with a dividend of ₹12 per share and EPS of ₹40. The dividend payout ratio is:
e: Payout ratio = DPS/EPS = 12/40 = 30%. Dividend yield would be 12/480 = 2.5%.

t: In India, mutual funds are regulated by SEBI under the:
o: Companies Act, 2013
Insurance Act, 1938
Banking Regulation Act, 1949
SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
e: The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 govern the sponsor, trustee, AMC and scheme structure of Indian mutual funds.

t: A mutual fund scheme has total assets of ₹520 crore, liabilities of ₹20 crore and 25 crore units outstanding. Its NAV per unit is:
In a life insurance contract, insurable interest must exist:
o: At the time of the claim only
At inception of the policy
Both at inception and at claim
At renewal each year
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Life: at inception only. Marine: at the time of loss. Fire and motor: at both inception and loss.

t: A put option with a strike price of ₹300 is held when the underlying share trades at ₹320. The option is:
o: In the money
At the money
Deep in the money
Out of the money
e: A put is in the money only when the strike exceeds the spot; here spot (320) is above strike (300), so the put has no intrinsic value.

t: Under IRDAI's guidelines on credit default swaps (CDS), insurers are permitted to participate in the CDS market only as:
o: Protection buyers, to hedge credit risk on corporate bonds they hold
Protection sellers, to earn premium income
Market makers for CDS contracts
Both buyers and sellers without restriction
e: IRDAI allows insurers to buy credit protection on bonds in their portfolio; selling protection (taking on credit risk) is not permitted.

t: The initial amount deposited with the exchange when a futures position is opened is called:
o: Initial margin
Maintenance margin
Variation margin
Option premium
e: Initial margin is the up-front deposit; maintenance margin is the minimum balance and variation margin is the daily top-up when losses reduce the balance.

t: A 3-year bond of face value ₹1,000 with a 10% annual coupon is priced when the market yield is 8%. Its price is approximately:
Approximate yield to maturity of a bond can be estimated as:
o: [Coupon + (Face value − Price)/Years to maturity] / [(Face value + Price)/2]
Coupon / Face value
(Face value − Price) / Coupon
Coupon × Years to maturity / Price
e: The approximation adds the annualised capital gain (or loss) to the coupon and divides by the average of face value and price.

t: Under IRDAI valuation norms, investments in real estate (property) held by an insurer are valued at:
o: Market value determined daily
Historical cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment, with a revaluation at least once in three years
Face value of the title deed
Rental income capitalised at the bank rate
e: Investment property is carried at cost less depreciation and revalued at least once every three years; the revaluation change goes to the revaluation reserve.

t: Which of the following best describes the 'discontinued policy fund' under IRDAI's ULIP regulations?
o: A segregated fund into which the fund value of policies discontinued during the lock-in period is transferred, earning a minimum guaranteed return
A fund that invests only in equities to maximise returns
The insurer's shareholders' fund
A fund used to pay agents' commissions
e: On discontinuance within the lock-in, the fund value (less discontinuance charge) is moved to the discontinued policy fund, which must earn at least the minimum rate prescribed by IRDAI.

t: A ULIP policyholder switches ₹60,000 from a debt fund (NAV ₹18.00) to an equity fund (NAV ₹30.00) with no switching charge. Units cancelled in the debt fund and units created in the equity fund are respectively:
e: Debt units cancelled = 60,000/18 = 3,333.33; equity units created = 60,000/30 = 2,000.

t: Non-disclosure of a material fact by the proposer makes the contract:
o: Void ab initio
Voidable at the option of the insurer
Illegal
Automatically continued on revised terms
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Breach of utmost good faith renders the contract voidable, not void; the insurer may elect to avoid it (subject to Section 45 for life).

t: Under IRDAI's unit-linked regulations, premiums received by the insurer up to the cut-off time of 3.00 p.m. on a business day are allotted units at:
o: The closing NAV of the next business day
The NAV of the previous business day
The NAV prevailing at the time of receipt
The closing NAV of the same day
e: Requests received before 3.00 p.m. get the same day's closing NAV; those received later get the next business day's NAV.

t: An Indian investor buying US Treasury bonds would be exposed to which additional risk compared with buying Indian G-secs?
o: Higher default risk of the US government
Exchange rate risk on conversion of dollar receipts to rupees
Lack of any secondary market
Daily mark-to-market margin calls
e: Foreign bonds add currency risk; US Treasuries are highly liquid and regarded as free of default risk.

t: Interest rate parity implies that the currency of the country with the higher interest rate will:
o: Trade at a forward premium against the lower-interest currency
Have the same forward and spot rates
Trade at a forward discount against the lower-interest currency
Appreciate in the spot market immediately
e: Under covered interest parity, the forward rate offsets the interest differential, so the high-interest currency is at a forward discount (e.g. the rupee against the dollar).
